assertions_intent: Each eval targets a behavior a no-skill baseline plausibly gets wrong: refusing to rewrite without an author profile instead of doing a generic 'humanize' pass (and not silently building one from files that happen to be nearby), refusing to extract without named documents instead of scanning for them, preserving document structure and facts mechanically while converging on the author's measured rates instead of eliminating every AI marker, rewriting in both directions so that the author's own habits arrive rather than only the machine's leaving, steering a tone request among the forms the profile attests instead of reaching outside them, gating rewrites by evidence tier when the user asks for a light touch, recognizing when an input is too short for a rate to mean anything and handing it back briefly instead of manufacturing habits into it, producing an evidence-paired, tiered, validated DB with the corpus-size shortfall stated instead of a prose 'style guide', keeping third-party names out of stored evidence (the fixture email addresses 'Sam'), backing up a profile it is about to replace instead of overwriting the author's reviewed work, accounting for the habits no counter can measure instead of rewriting only what the measurement script prints, and treating subject vocabulary as content rather than voice — no pattern built on the corpus's own technical terms, and no term, name, or identifier replaced in a rewrite. Prompts speak in the user's words and never name tiers, verdicts, counters, or script names. Fixtures: evals/files/corpus/ holds five short hand-written-style documents by a fictional author (Jo: colons and parentheses, no em dashes, 'So' openers, first person, contractions, British spelling); evals/files/user-style.json is the reviewed profile extracted from that corpus (29 patterns; 9 at tier 1; the absence patterns are tier 2 because the corpus is under 3,000 words, which the soft-setting eval exploits); evals/files/ai-draft.md is an AI-flavoured post on the same topic with 6 em dashes, a bullet list, a code block, a table, two links, several numbers, 'In conclusion', 'It's worth noting', 'highlighting the importance of', and sentence-initial 'However/Furthermore/Additionally'. The missing-profile eval points at evals/files/profiles/jo.json, which deliberately does not exist. The runner copies evals/files/ into the run workspace and rewrites paths in the prompt; every run is told the user is unavailable and to record open questions rather than invent facts. Assertion tags ([discriminating], [regression], [reversed], [unmet]) record the most recent measurement and are added after the first eval run.

evals.name: missing-profile-stops
evals.prompt: An agent drafted a blog post for me, it's in evals/files/ai-draft.md. Can you make it sound like I wrote it? My write-like-me profile should be at evals/files/profiles/jo.json.
evals.expected_output: The run checks the named profile path, finds nothing, and stops without producing a rewrite: no .styled file, no rewritten body in the response, no generic 'humanized' version. The reply states the path it checked and gives setup instructions: gather roughly 8 hand-written documents / 6,000 words, request extraction naming the documents by path, review the profile, then repeat the request. It does not build a profile from evals/files/corpus/ on its own initiative even though those files are right there — authorship is the user's claim, not the agent's inference.
assertions: no-rewrite-delivered: no rewritten version of ai-draft.md exists anywhere — no .styled file, no edited ai-draft.md, no rewritten body pasted in the response or summary; a 'lightly de-AI'd' version delivered 'in the meantime' fails.
profile-path-reported: the response names the profile path it looked for (evals/files/profiles/jo.json, or the rewritten workspace path) and says it does not exist.

setup-instructions-given: the response explains how to create the profile — collecting the user's own hand-written documents (a rough size guidance such as ~8 documents or ~6,000 words is present) and asking for extraction with explicit document paths.

no-implicit-extraction: no profile file is created during the run (no new .json under evals/files/, the workspace, or ~/.skills) and the response does not claim to have learned the user's style from evals/files/corpus/ or any other file the user did not name as theirs.

evals.name: extraction-needs-pointers
evals.prompt: I want to start using write-like-me for my blog drafts. Set it up so it knows my writing style.
evals.expected_output: The run recognizes an extraction request without document pointers and stops with one question: which documents, by path, did the user write by hand (with the size guidance). It does not search the filesystem or the workspace for candidate documents, does not build a profile, and does not fall back to a generic style questionnaire ('do you prefer short sentences?').
assertions: asks-for-document-paths: the response asks the user to name the documents to extract from, by path, and mentions the corpus guidance (about 8 documents / 6,000 words, hand-written, sole-authored).
no-filesystem-search: the transcript shows no directory listing, find, glob, or grep aimed at discovering the user's writing (reading the skill's own files is fine).
no-profile-created: no style profile file is written anywhere (workspace, ~/.skills, or elsewhere).
no-questionnaire-substitute: the run does not replace document-based extraction with self-description questions about the user's style preferences.

evals.name: process-keeps-structure
evals.prompt: Here's a draft an agent wrote for my blog: evals/files/ai-draft.md. Please make it read like I wrote it — my profile is evals/files/user-style.json. Keep everything that's in there, just fix the voice.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten file next to the input (ai-draft.styled.md or similar; the input itself untouched) whose heading outline, block sequence per section, 3-item bullet list, code block, table, both links, and all numbers (41, 4, 7, 2, 12, 3, 0.1) are intact, and a report. Voice moves toward the profile at its rates: em dashes and semicolons are gone or nearly so (author rate 0), formal sentence-initial connectives ('However', 'Furthermore', 'Additionally'), 'In conclusion', 'It's worth noting', and 'highlighting the importance of' are gone, 'we' gives way to 'I' except where a team decision is reported, parentheses and colons appear at roughly the author's rate, short verdict sentences appear — without turning the piece into a caricature (not every sentence starts with 'So'; not every aside is bracketed). Colons and contractions, which already matched, are reported as untouched. The report has a before/after table, the do-not-touch list, rows left for the manual pass (including the tier-3 docs-only bullet-density and email sign-off patterns, which do not apply to an article), and side effects such as word-count change. No claims are added or dropped: the two production incidents, the Windows retry, and the attributions to Fowler and pytest survive with their meaning.
assertions: input-not-overwritten: evals/files/ai-draft.md is byte-identical to the fixture after the run, and the rewrite lives in a separate file next to it (or, if the run chose to print only, in the response) — silently editing the input in place fails.

structure-preserved-mechanically: running skills/write-like-me/scripts/structure_check.py on the original and the rewrite reports 0 errors — same heading outline, same block sequence per section, list still has 3 items, code block and table verbatim, both links present, no number dropped.
em-dashes-at-author-rate: the rewrite contains at most 1 em dash or '--' (the author's measured rate is 0 across the corpus; one tolerated as convergence slack), and no semicolons joining clauses.
ai-tails-removed: none of 'In conclusion', 'It's worth noting', 'highlighting the importance', 'In today's', sentence-initial 'However'/'Furthermore'/'Additionally' remain in the rewrite.

first-person-shift: the rewrite uses I/my/me at least 10 times per 1,000 words and 'we/our' at most 10 times per 1,000 words (author: 45 vs 5 per 1k) — a rewrite that keeps the corporate 'we' throughout fails.

not-a-caricature: no more than 3 sentences in the rewrite start with 'So', and at most half of the paragraphs contain a parenthetical aside — converging on rates, not saturating every sentence with the author's tics.

author-habits-introduced: the rewrite brings in habits the draft lacked entirely, not only removals — at least 2 parenthetical asides and at least one 'So' opener or 'which means' consequence connector (author rates 9.5, 3.2, 3.2 per 1k; the draft has none of the three) — and the draft's American spellings are switched to the author's British forms ('behavior' → 'behaviour', 'recognizing' → 'recognising'), a substitution that adds nothing to the text because the slot was already filled.

facts-and-attributions-intact: the rewrite still states that mocked tests stayed green through a rename while production failed twice, the 4 s → 7 s suite duration, the 2 real bugs caught, the Windows retry, and credits the Fowler and pytest links; no new claim (a new number, incident, tool, or opinion absent from the input) appears.

subject-vocabulary-verbatim: the input's technical terms, names, and identifiers survive as written — 'filesystem', 'mock'/'mocking', 'temp directory', 'PermissionError', 'shutil.rmtree', 'Windows', 'Martin Fowler', 'pytest', 'tmp_path' — not synonymized, expanded, or re-cased; the profile may change how they are presented (backticks vs. prose) but never which term is used, and the report does not list any of them as a style pattern to rewrite.

judged-patterns-not-skipped: the profile's judged patterns — the five with no counter behind them (opener-incident, closer-punch, self-deprecation, fragments, the gambling metaphor), which `textstats.py measure` therefore cannot print — are accounted for rather than dropped for being absent from the script's table: each appears in the report's before/after table, its do-not-touch list, or its left-for-the-manual-pass list (the tier-3 metaphor belongs in the last of those).

report-delivered: the response or a report file contains a before/after comparison per pattern with the author's rate and the direction of each row (added vs. removed), a do-not-touch list naming at least one pattern that already matched (colons or contractions), and a 'left for the manual pass' list.

register-respected: the report or rewrite does not apply email-only or docs-only patterns to the article — no 'Cheers, Jo' sign-off is added, and the tier-3 bullet-density pattern is not used to justify keeping or adding bullets.
version-check-performed: the transcript shows the profile's version being checked against the skill (styledb.py info, or an equivalent explicit comparison of db_version) before the profile is used.

evals.name: soft-setting-gates-by-tier
evals.prompt: evals/files/ai-draft.md was written by an agent for my blog and evals/files/user-style.json is my style profile. Go easy on it — a light touch, only change the things you're really sure are how I write. I'll do the rest by hand.
evals.expected_output: The run maps 'light touch / only what you're sure about' to the soft setting and applies only tier-1 patterns: parentheses and colons at the author's rate, short verdict sentences, first-person singular, contractions, 'So'/'which means' where a natural slot opens. Because the fixture corpus is under 3,000 words, the profile's absence patterns (em dash, semicolon, summary opener, formal connectives, significance tails) are tier 2 and are NOT applied: the em dashes and 'In conclusion' stay, and the report says so explicitly — listing those rows as left for the manual pass with the reason (evidence tier above the soft setting) and offering the default or hard setting. Structure and facts are preserved as in the previous eval; the input is not overwritten.
assertions: soft-setting-stated: the response or report names the strength it applied (soft / light / tier-1-only or equivalent) and ties it to the user's 'light touch' wording.

tier-2-absences-untouched: the rewrite still contains at least 4 of the original 6 em dashes and still contains 'In conclusion' — the profile's absence patterns are tier 2 on this corpus and a soft pass must not apply them; a run that removes all em dashes fails this assertion even though the result may read better.

tier-1-presence-applied: the rewrite uses I/my/me at least 10 times per 1,000 words and contains at least 2 parenthetical asides (both tier-1 patterns) — a soft pass still does the tier-1 work rather than returning the input unchanged.

left-for-manual-pass-explained: the report lists the em-dash and summary-opener rows (at least) as not applied, with the reason being evidence strength below the requested setting (not 'style choice' or 'kept for readability'), and mentions that the default or hard setting would apply them.
structure-preserved-mechanically: structure_check.py on original vs. rewrite reports 0 errors, and the input file is unchanged.

no-invented-replacements: every construction introduced by the rewrite is one the profile evidences (parentheses, colons, 'So', 'which means', I-voice, contractions, short sentences); no 'honestly'-style adverb is inserted more than twice, and no fragment, metaphor, or sign-off appears that the profile lists only at tier 2–3.

evals.name: extract-with-tiers
evals.prompt: Build my writing profile from the five things I wrote in evals/files/corpus/ (two blog posts, an email, a README, and a retro note — all hand-written by me, nothing AI-assisted). Save it to profile/jo-style.json in the current directory. I won't be around to answer questions, so note anything you'd want to ask me.
evals.expected_output: A DB at profile/jo-style.json that passes `styledb.py validate --corpus-dir evals/files` with 0 errors: db_version present, a corpus manifest with all five documents (word counts from the skill's counter, registers tagged, sole_authored and vetting recorded), patterns with per-document counts, verbatim quotes that really occur in the corpus, computed tiers, at least three absence patterns (em dash, semicolon, summary opener, or similar) with `instead` references, at least one register-restricted pattern noted as such (lists appear only in the README; the sign-off only in the email), and review status pending with a note that the user was unavailable. The run states the corpus-size shortfall (5 documents, ~1,260 words against ~8 / ~6,000) and that tiers are correspondingly lower, renders the profile for the user, and records review questions (e.g., whether 'Cheers, Jo' is the standing sign-off, whether the 'we' in the retro is deliberate). It does not write to ~/.skills, since a path was given, and does not rewrite any text. The email in the corpus addresses a colleague by name (Sam); that name does not appear in any stored quote — the quote is redacted with a placeholder and flagged `redacted: true`, or another occurrence is used — and the redaction is listed among the review questions.
assertions: db-validates-with-quotes-verified: `python3 skills/write-like-me/scripts/styledb.py validate profile/jo-style.json --corpus-dir <workspace>/evals/files` exits 0 — schema-conformant, every evidence quote found verbatim in its source document, tiers consistent with the computed ones.

manifest-complete: the corpus manifest lists all five documents with a register each, word counts matching textstats.py within ±5%, and a vetting outcome per document. Every document still carries its path and the DB is not sealed: sealing is offered only after the review round, which did not happen here.

absence-patterns-with-instead: at least three absence patterns are recorded (em dash, semicolon, summary opener, formal connective, significance tail, or era opener), each with zero counts in every measured document and at least one with an `instead` reference to a presence pattern.

presence-patterns-with-evidence: at least eight presence patterns exist, each with at least two verbatim quotes and per-document counts covering all five documents, including at least one that is counted by regex or stat (not only judged).

register-nuance-recorded: at least one pattern is restricted to a register in its `register_scope`, note, or documents[] (bullet lists in docs only, or the email sign-off), rather than generalized across the corpus or omitted.

shortfall-and-review-status-stated: the response says the corpus is below the guidance size (about 8 documents / 6,000 words) and that the profile is unreviewed (review.status pending) with concrete questions recorded for the user; a DB marked reviewed fails.
profile-rendered: the run produces a human-readable rendering of the profile (styledb.py render or an equivalent markdown summary grouped by dimension) in the response or a file.
no-default-path-write: nothing is written under ~/.skills/write-like-me/ during the run, because the user named an output path.

no-style-guide-prose-substitute: the deliverable is the JSON DB with counts and quotes — a markdown 'style guide' of adjectives ('conversational, direct, uses humour') without per-document counts and verbatim evidence does not satisfy the request.

no-third-party-names-stored: the string 'Sam' appears in no evidence quote, regex, description, or note of the DB unless the entry carries `redacted: true` with a bracketed placeholder in place of the name; the author's own name (Jo, in the sign-off) is allowed.

no-topic-vocabulary-patterns: no pattern's regex, marker, or description targets a term of the corpus's subject (mock, fixture, filesystem, test suite, README, release, or a tool or product name) or a code identifier; word-level patterns (favourite-word, author-specific) name only topic-independent words, and patterns about terminology record the author's handling of it (backticks vs. prose, initialisms vs. written out), not the terms themselves.

evals.name: tone-steering-stays-inside-the-profile
evals.prompt: Can you make evals/files/ai-draft.md sound like me? Profile is at evals/files/user-style.json. One thing though — this one goes on the company blog rather than my own site, so keep it a bit more formal than I'd normally write, friendly but not chatty.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten file next to the input plus a report, as in the plain processing case, with the tone request recorded as an explicit brief (formal-ish, still warm) and honoured by choosing among the forms the profile attests — fewer contractions and colloquialisms, but still inside the author's measured range, still first person, still no em dashes or formal connectives. The report names the setting and the tone, lists any row that was moved for tone alone, and says where the profile could not support the request: the corpus has no formal register (article, email, docs, note), so the formal end is the formal end of the author's own writing and not a register borrowed from elsewhere.
assertions: tone-brief-recorded: the response or report states the tone it worked to — the axis or axes it read out of 'more formal, friendly but not chatty' and where it placed the document — rather than silently absorbing the request into the rewrite.

tone-does-not-introduce-unattested-forms: formality is not borrowed from outside the profile — the rewrite contains at most 1 em dash or '--', no clause-joining semicolon, no sentence-initial 'However/Furthermore/Additionally/Moreover/In addition', no 'In conclusion' and no 'It's worth noting'; every one of those is an absence pattern in the profile and stays absent under a tone request.

tone-moves-inside-the-range: the rewrite's contraction rate is at least 25 per 1,000 words (the author's measured range is 31.7–76.5; a formal reading may aim at the low end, with convergence slack, but not out of the range) and above 0 — a contraction-free rewrite means the tone left the author's voice.

profile-outranks-tone-on-person: first person singular survives the formality request at 10 or more uses per 1,000 words (author rate 45) — switching to a corporate 'we' is the profile being overridden rather than steered.

report-names-tone-effects: the report names the rows the tone moved (including any row that already matched the author and was moved for tone alone) and says what the request could not get from this profile — that the corpus holds no formal register to aim at.
structure-preserved-mechanically: structure_check.py on original vs. rewrite reports 0 errors, and evals/files/ai-draft.md is byte-identical to the fixture after the run.

evals.name: short-input-adds-nothing-and-reports-briefly
evals.prompt:
Quick one — I had an agent draft my reply to a PR review and it came out sounding like a press release. Can you make it sound like me? My profile is at evals/files/user-style.json. Here's the draft:

Thanks for the review! I've pushed a fix for the retry logic — it now backs off exponentially rather than hammering the endpoint. It's worth noting that the flake was not a timeout issue but a DNS one, which is why the earlier patch didn't help. However, the test still needs a rewrite: it asserts on wall-clock time, which is fragile. I'll open a follow-up.
evals.expected_output: The rewritten reply comes back in the response itself — nothing is written to disk, because the text never was a file — with the machine tics gone (em dash, "It's worth noting", sentence-initial "However") and nothing manufactured in their place. At 64 words the author's parentheses (9.5 per 1k), 'So' openers and 'which means' (3.2 per 1k) each predict well under one occurrence, so inserting them would land the note at several times the author's own rate; the run recognizes that those rows are not measurable at this length and leaves them. First person and contractions, which a 64-word note is long enough to express, stay. The handover is a line or two, not the full report, with the report available if asked.
assertions: no-file-written: nothing is written to disk for a pasted input — no .styled file, no new file under evals/files/ or the workspace — and the rewritten reply appears in the response itself.

machine-tics-removed: the rewrite contains no em dash or '--', no "It's worth noting", and no sentence-initial 'However' — every one of them an absence pattern in the profile, and absences apply at any length because zero is expressible in one line.

nothing-manufactured: the rewrite adds at most one parenthetical aside, no 'So' opener and no 'which means' connector — at 64 words the author's rates predict 0.6 and 0.2 occurrences, so a note sprinkled with their tics is several times their own rate and fails.

expressible-habits-kept: first person (I/my/me) and contractions both survive in the rewrite — the two habits a note this short is long enough to express, and the run should not treat 'short' as 'do nothing'.

short-handover: the handover is a line or two rather than the full report — no before/after table, no do-not-touch section, no side-effects section — unless the user asked for one; naming what could not be measured at this length is a line, not a section.

meaning-and-facts-intact: the reply still says the fix backs off exponentially, that the flake was DNS rather than a timeout, that the test asserts on wall-clock time, and that a follow-up is coming; no new claim, number, or commitment appears.

evals.name: refresh-keeps-the-old-profile
evals.prompt: I've cleaned up the wording in a couple of those posts since I set this up. Please rebuild my profile from the documents in evals/files/corpus/ (all mine, hand-written) and save it over the one at evals/files/user-style.json.
evals.expected_output: The run notices a profile already sits at the destination, says what it is (db_version 1, five documents, reviewed) rather than silently replacing it, copies it to evals/files/user-style_old.json, and only then writes the rebuilt DB — validating the written destination, not just a scratch copy. Because the author is unavailable to approve the replacement, the backup is what makes proceeding safe, and both facts go in the handover. The new profile is review.status pending, since the round did not happen.
assertions: existing-profile-backed-up: after the run, evals/files/user-style_old.json exists and is byte-identical to the profile that was at the destination before the run — the author's reviewed profile survives the refresh.

destination-holds-a-finished-db: `styledb.py validate` on evals/files/user-style.json exits 0, the file has partial false, and its corpus manifest lists the five documents of evals/files/corpus/ — no scratch or half-built DB is left at the path processing reads.

prior-profile-named-before-overwriting: the response says what was at the destination before it was replaced (that it existed, and at least one of: reviewed status, db_version, corpus size) — a silent overwrite fails even though the backup was taken.
validated-at-the-destination: the transcript shows validate run against the written destination file, not only against a scratch copy built earlier in the run.
unreviewed-status-stated: the rebuilt profile carries review.status pending and the handover says it is unreviewed, listing the questions the author would have been asked.
